summary: This Best Current Practice document describes security measures that can and should be deployed around the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), the protocol almost exclusively used to exchange routing information between networks, since its central role makes its security important.

plainLanguage.summary: BGP is how the Internet learns which network can reach which block of addresses, and it does not check whether the announcements it carries are sensible. This document is the operator's checklist: how to lock down the router that speaks BGP, how to keep the session between two routers from being hijacked, and which address ranges and routes a network should accept and refuse.

subtitle: The operator's checklist for keeping BGP sessions, routes and routers from being abused.

tldr.problem: BGP is the protocol almost exclusively used to exchange routing information between networks, but it carries no mechanism of its own for deciding whether the routes it exchanges conform to the guidelines the Internet community has agreed on.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gathers the existing practice into one policy: protect the BGP speaker and its TCP session with access control lists, TTL security and session authentication; filter the prefixes that are received and announced; and control the flow of routing information with AS path filters, route flap dampening, maximum prefix limits and community scrubbing.
tldr.outcome: The result is a document that network operators can use to apply a coherent BGP policy rather than a set of disconnected tricks. RFC 7454 is a Best Current Practice and, according to the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

facts.label: IPv6 filter refresh window
facts.value: Within a maximum of one month

facts.label: Route with no ROA
facts.value: Accept it, but give the route a low preference

today: RFC 7454 is a Best Current Practice and, according to the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. It remains the reference for generic BGP operational security guidance.

sections.title: BGP Policies Are Not Built In
sections.content:
The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), specified in RFC 4271, is the protocol used in the Internet to exchange routing information between network domains. BGP does not include any mechanism that controls whether the routes exchanged conform to the various guidelines defined by the Internet community. This document fills that gap. It summarizes the guidelines that already exist in common practice and helps network administrators apply them as one coherent policy.

The advice falls into two broad groups. The first protects the BGP speaker and the session it runs over, so that an outside party cannot take the session over or flood the router. The second controls the flow of routing information itself: which IP prefixes, meaning blocks of addresses, are accepted and which are announced, how many routes a peer may send, and what happens to routes that keep changing.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP tells the Internet which network reaches which address range, but it does not check whether the announcements it carries are sensible. This document is the checklist for the operator who has to decide what to accept and what to send.

sections.title: Scope and Local Exceptions
sections.content:
The guidelines are written for generic Internet BGP peerings, and they are written as advice rather than as rules every network must follow. Autonomous Systems can always agree on exceptions to a common framework for local needs, and a session may be configured in a way that differs from the recommendations here. The RFC accepts that, with one warning attached: every configured exception might have an impact on the entire inter-domain routing environment, and network administrators SHOULD carefully appraise this impact before implementation.

Section 3 defines the terms used later on. An ACL is an Access Control List, an ASN an Autonomous System Number, an IRR an Internet Routing Registry, an IXP an Internet Exchange Point, an LIR a Local Internet Registry, an RIR a Regional Internet Registry, PMTUD Path MTU Discovery and uRPF Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding. A Tier 1 transit provider is an IP transit provider that can reach any network on the Internet without purchasing transit services. Downstream means any network that is downstream, whether a provider or a customer network; upstream means any network that is upstream.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are a starting point, not a law. Two networks can agree to do something different, but the RFC asks them to think about what that does to the rest of the Internet first.

sections.title: Protecting the BGP Speaker
sections.content:
The router that speaks BGP has to be protected from attempts to subvert the BGP session. That protection SHOULD be achieved with an Access Control List (ACL) that discards all packets directed to TCP port 179 on the local device when they are sourced from an address that is not known or permitted to become a BGP neighbour. The RFC explains why the protection TCP itself offers is not always enough: it is sometimes run in control-plane software, and in the absence of ACLs it is possible to attack a BGP speaker by simply sending a high volume of connection requests to it.

If the hardware supports it, an ACL specific to the control plane of the router SHOULD be used, such as a receive-ACL or control-plane policing, so that data-plane filters do not have to be configured for packets that are merely transiting the router and never reach the control plane. If the hardware cannot do that, interface ACLs can be used to block packets addressed to the local router. Some routers automatically program such an ACL when BGP is configured; on other devices this ACL has to be configured and maintained manually or with scripts.

Beyond strict filtering, rate limiting MAY be configured for accepted BGP traffic, permitting only a certain quantity of bits per second, or packets per second, of BGP traffic to reach the control plane. That protects the BGP router control plane in case the amount of BGP traffic surpasses the capabilities of the platform. The RFC notes that filtering and rate limiting of control-plane traffic is a wider topic than BGP alone, and points to RFC 6192 for a more detailed recommendation on protecting the router's control plane.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep the door locked on the port BGP uses, so that only addresses you have agreed may open a session. Then limit how much traffic that door lets through at once, so a flood cannot overwhelm the router.

sections.title: Protecting the BGP Session
sections.content:
Attacks on the TCP session that carries BGP, for example spoofed TCP RST packets, could bring down a BGP peering. After a successful ARP spoofing attack, or another similar man-in-the-middle attack, the attacker might even be able to inject packets into the TCP stream, which is a routing attack.

Several mechanisms exist. MD5 protection of the TCP session header, described in RFC 2385, was the first such mechanism. It has been obsoleted by the TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO, RFC 5925), which offers stronger protection. MD5 is still the most used mechanism because of its availability in vendors' equipment, but TCP-AO SHOULD be preferred when it is implemented. IPsec could also be used for session protection, but at the time of publication there was not enough experience of the impact of using IPsec for BGP peerings for the RFC to define guidelines.

The RFC is deliberately relaxed about requiring any of this. The drawback of TCP session protection is additional configuration and management overhead for the maintenance of authentication information such as MD5 passwords. Protection of TCP sessions used by BGP is therefore NOT REQUIRED, even when peerings are established over shared networks where spoofing can be done, such as at an IXP. Operators are RECOMMENDED to consider the trade-offs and to apply TCP session protection where appropriate. One thing is recommended without exception: administrators SHOULD block spoofed packets, meaning packets with a source IP address belonging to their own address space, at all edges of their network, following RFC 2827 and RFC 3704. That protects the TCP session used by Internal BGP from attackers outside the Autonomous System.

Section 5.2 adds the Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (GTSM, RFC 5082). Instead of sending TCP packets with a TTL value of 1, the BGP speakers send them with a TTL value of 255, and the receiver checks that the value equals 255. Since it is impossible to send an IP packet with a TTL of 255 to an IP host that is not directly connected, TTL security effectively prevents all spoofing attacks coming from third parties that are not directly connected to the same subnet as the BGP-speaking routers. The RFC says administrators SHOULD implement TTL security on directly connected BGP peerings. It can be applied to multi-hop peerings as well, with a TTL value configured to match the distance between the speakers, but it is less effective there, because anyone inside the TTL diameter could spoof the TTL. Like MD5 protection, TTL security has to be configured on both ends of a BGP session.
sections.plainLanguage: Two tricks protect the connection itself. One makes sure the packets really came from the neighbouring router, by using a secret or a stronger cryptographic check. The other makes it hard to fake a packet from far away, by insisting that every packet on the session arrives with its hop limit set to 255.

sections.title: Prefix Filtering
sections.content:
The RFC calls control of the prefixes that are received and advertised the main aspect of securing BGP. Prefixes exchanged between peers are controlled with inbound and outbound filters that can match on IP prefixes, on AS paths as described in Section 9, or on any other attribute of a BGP prefix, such as BGP communities as described in Section 11.

Section 6.1 lists the filter families. Special-purpose prefixes come first: the IANA IPv4 and IPv6 Special-Purpose Address registries maintain the lists and their routing scope, and prefixes with the value "False" in the "Global" column SHOULD be discarded on Internet BGP peerings. Unallocated prefixes come next. IANA allocates prefixes to RIRs, which allocate to LIRs, and it is wise not to accept prefixes that nobody has been allocated. This needs constant updates, because prefixes are continually allocated, so automation of such filters is key; administrators SHOULD NOT consider these solutions if they cannot keep the filters updated, because the damage would probably be worse than the intended security policy. For IPv4 there is nothing to check, because IANA has allocated the whole address space; for IPv6, administrators can build the list of IANA-allocated prefixes dynamically, and SHOULD ensure that all IPv6 prefix filters are updated within a maximum of one month after any change in the IANA list.

A more precise check looks at whether the prefixes are being originated or transited by autonomous systems entitled to do so, using either Internet Routing Registries or the SIDR infrastructure. IRR entries describe routing policy using Routing Policy Specification Language objects as described in RFC 4012, and the RFC notes that such lists are not necessarily complete. Filters computed this way should be refreshed regularly, and refreshing them on a daily basis SHOULD be considered, because routing changes sometimes have to be made in a hurry and registries may be updated at the last moment. The cost is configuration size: this can quickly add tens of thousands of configuration lines for some important peers. The SIDR infrastructure, described in RFC 6480, offers origin validation, described in RFC 6811, which is operational, and path validation through BGPsec, which is still an ongoing work item and therefore cannot be implemented. If origin validation is implemented, the rules of RFC 7115 apply: a valid ROA means the prefix should be accepted, an invalid ROA means it should be discarded, and no ROA means the prefix should be accepted but the route should be given a low preference.

Three more families are about the shape of the prefix rather than its owner. Prefixes that are too specific: the RFC does not judge the right level of specificity, but notes that the RIPE community has documented that IPv4 prefixes longer than /24 and IPv6 prefixes longer than /48 are generally neither announced nor accepted on the Internet. Prefixes belonging to the local AS and its downstreams: a network SHOULD filter its own prefixes on peerings with all its peers in the inbound direction, so that local traffic cannot leak over an external peering if somebody else announces the same prefix, though such filters SHOULD NOT be applied in some multihoming scenarios, where they would break the desired redundancy. IXP LAN prefixes: a network on an IXP SHOULD NOT accept more-specific prefixes for the IXP LAN prefix from any of its external BGP peers, because that may create a black hole for connectivity to the IXP LAN. Finally the default route: the 0.0.0.0/0 prefix and the ::/0 prefix are typically not intended to be accepted or advertised except in specific customer and provider configurations, and general filtering outside of those is RECOMMENDED.

Sections 6.2 and 6.3 turn the list into policy per kind of peer. It is RECOMMENDED that each Autonomous System configures rules for advertised and received routes at all its borders, which protects the network and its peer even in case of misconfiguration. With Internet peers there are two options: a loose one that checks the families listed above without consulting the RIR allocations, and a strict one that verifies that advertisements strictly conform to what is declared in the routing registries, with a warning that registries are not always accurate and that the reader should check the impact of the filter before applying a strict policy. With customers the inbound policy is straightforward: only customer prefixes should be accepted and all others discarded. With upstream providers the inbound filtering is the same as for Internet peers, except for the default route. A leaf network applies the filters corresponding to the routes it is requesting from its upstream, and will most likely only announce its local routes.
sections.plainLanguage: The core of the document is a list of address blocks a network should refuse to hear about: blocks reserved for special uses, blocks nobody has been allocated, blocks more specific than the Internet normally uses, its own blocks, and the catch-all route. The filters have to be rebuilt as allocations change, so the RFC insists on automating them.

sections.title: Route Flap Dampening and Maximum Prefixes
sections.content:
The BGP route flap dampening mechanism gives penalties to routes each time they change in the BGP routing table. It was created to protect the entire Internet from multiple events that impact a single network. Studies have shown that implementations of route flap dampening could cause more harm than benefit, and for that reason the RIPE community recommended against using it. Later studies proposed new thresholds in order to make the solution usable, which are described in RFC 7196. This document RECOMMENDS following the IETF and RIPE recommendations and using BGP route flap dampening with the adjusted configured thresholds.

On maximum prefixes, the RFC says it is RECOMMENDED to configure a limit on the number of routes to be accepted from a peer. From peers, it is RECOMMENDED to have a limit lower than the number of routes in the Internet, which shuts down the BGP peering if the peer suddenly advertises the full table. Administrators can also configure different limits for each peer, according to the number of routes they are supposed to advertise, plus some headroom to permit growth. From upstreams that provide full routing, it is RECOMMENDED to have a limit higher than the number of routes in the Internet; a limit is still useful in order to protect the network, and in particular the routers' memory, if too many routes are sent by the upstream, and it should be chosen according to the number of routes the routers can actually handle.

It is important to review the configured limits regularly, because the Internet can change quickly over time. Some vendors propose mechanisms that have two thresholds: the higher number specified shuts the peering down, while the first threshold only triggers a log and can be used to passively adjust the limits based on observations made on the network.
sections.plainLanguage: Two more limits protect the router. One penalises a route that keeps flapping, so a single unstable network cannot disturb the whole Internet. The other caps how many routes a peer may send, so a misconfigured peer cannot fill the router's memory.

sections.title: AS Path, Next-Hop and Community Filters
sections.content:
Section 9 lists the practices for processing BGP AS paths. Administrators SHOULD accept from customers only 2-byte or 4-byte AS paths containing ASNs belonging to, or authorized to transit through, that customer; if they cannot build filtering expressions to implement that, they SHOULD consider accepting only path lengths relevant to the type of customer they have and SHOULD try to discourage excessive prepending in such paths. They SHOULD NOT accept prefixes with private AS numbers in the AS path unless the prefixes are from customers, with an exception for an upstream offering a service such as black-hole origination based on a private AS number. They SHOULD NOT accept prefixes when the first AS number in the AS path is not the one of the peer, unless the peering is done toward a BGP route server with transparent AS path handling, as on an IXP. They SHOULD NOT advertise prefixes with a nonempty AS path unless they intend to provide transit for them, nor advertise prefixes with upstream AS numbers in the AS path to their peering AS unless they intend to provide transit for those prefixes. Private AS numbers are conventionally used in private contexts, SHOULD NOT be used in advertisements to BGP peers that are not party to such arrangements, and SHOULD be stripped when received from peers that are not party to them. Finally, administrators SHOULD NOT override BGP's default behaviour, which is not to accept their own AS number in the AS path, and should study the impact carefully when considering an exception. When an ASN is renumbered, the rules described above may be adjusted for the duration of the migration, which is usually done by presenting the previous ASN to the peer.

Section 10 deals with the next hop. On a shared network such as an IXP, BGP can advertise prefixes with a third-party next hop, directing packets not to the peer that announced the prefix but somewhere else. That is a desirable property for BGP route-server setups, where the route server relays routing information but has neither the capacity nor the desire to receive the actual data packets. In direct peerings between ISPs it is undesirable, because one of the peers could trick the other into sending packets into a black hole, or to an unsuspecting third party who would then have to carry the traffic, and the root cause is hard to see without inspecting the BGP prefixes at the receiving router of the IXP. An inbound route policy SHOULD therefore be applied on IXP peerings, setting the next hop for accepted prefixes to the BGP peer IP address on the IXP LAN that sent the prefix. That policy SHOULD NOT be used on route-server peerings, or on peerings where third-party next hops are intentionally permitted. If Remote Triggered Black Holing (RFC 6666) is implemented, the policy should be adjusted so that a well-known next hop, statically routed to a null interface, can be applied to the routes that should be filtered, with peers able to exchange black-hole information through an agreed-upon BGP community.

Section 11 covers BGP communities, which are labels attached to routes. Administrators SHOULD scrub inbound communities whose number has their own number in the high-order bits, and allow only those communities that customers and peers can use as a signalling mechanism. They SHOULD NOT remove other communities applied on received routes, and in particular SHOULD NOT generally remove the no-export community, as it is usually announced by the peer for a certain purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: Three more filters look at the route rather than the address. One checks the list of networks the route has crossed, so a customer cannot claim traffic for somebody else's address range. One makes sure traffic is sent to the router that announced the route. One strips the private labels that networks use internally, so they do not leak outside.

sections.title: What This Document Does Not Cover
sections.content:
Section 12 says plainly that the whole document is about BGP operational security. It depicts best practices that one should adopt to secure BGP infrastructure: protecting the BGP router and the BGP sessions, adopting consistent BGP prefix and AS path filters, and configuring other options to secure the BGP network.

It also says what it does not do. The document does not aim to describe existing BGP implementations, their potential vulnerabilities, or the ways they handle errors. It does not detail how protection could be enforced against attack techniques using crafted packets. Appendix A is an example only. It walks through the case of an IXP in the RIPE region that is allocated an IPv4 /22 prefix and uses a /23 of it for the IXP LAN, which is the prefix its members use to configure their peerings, and which might also have an AS number of its own. Any IXP member should make sure it filters prefixes more specific than the IXP LAN prefix from all its EBGP peers, because receiving something like a /24 of it could seriously affect its routing. The IXP should originate its whole /22 and advertise it to its members, most likely from its BGP route servers, and the members should accept that prefix only if it passes the IRR-generated filters, and then advertise it to their downstreams.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC is a checklist of things to configure, not a study of how BGP fails. It does not describe how routers implement BGP today, and it does not explain in detail how the attacks it mentions work.
